extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in cognitive linguistics, humor studies, and computational humor
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and representation of 'forced reinterpretation' jokes: describing how a set-up leads to an initially dominant interpretation that a punchline forces the audience (or a character) to reinterpret, and how this can be modeled using nested viewpoints/mental spaces. Useful for analyzing, modeling, or designing jokes that rely on reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up then punchline forcing reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: “initial portion (the set-up) which appears to have one interpretation, followed by a final part (the punchline) which forces the audience (reader or hearer) to perceive a different interpretation of the set-up.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core pattern: construct a set-up that licenses a salient interpretation, then provide a punchline that is odd under that interpretation but sensible under an alternative. Examples: goldfish in a tank (lexical ambiguity), riddle-style fake question (pragmatic illocutionary ambiguity). The paper uses multiple examples (1)-(9) to illustrate variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage incongruity-resolution structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour often follows a two-stage process: first perceiving an incongruity, then resolving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: 'In the first stage, the audience perceives some incongruity; in the second stage this incongruity is resolved.' Widely influential as a general framework, but the paper notes disagreement about precise definitions of 'incongruity' and 'resolution'. Use this as a high-level explanatory rubric rather than a rigid checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up must admit multiple interpretations though one is initially dominant
rubrics_metrics.description: The stimulus (set-up) has more than one interpretation in its initial stages, but only one interpretation is perceived by the audience until the punchline reveals the alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design/analysis should identify the competing interpretations and explain why one interpretation is favored (salience factors are noted but not the paper's focus). Examples include lexical ambiguity (tank), pragmatic ambiguity (fake riddles), and non-linguistic ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation can occur in any accessible (nested) viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: “the revised interpretation may occur in any nested viewpoint, and need not be adopted by the audience as a factually correct interpretation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model reinterpretation as a change within a viewpoint (mental space) accessible to the audience: the audience's own viewpoint, a narrative viewpoint, or a story character's viewpoint. The crucial condition is accessibility (nesting), not location in the audience's direct belief-set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation aims at coherence more than veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift in interpretation is not always from factually incorrect to factually correct; it may be from an incoherent to a coherent reading (coherence over veracity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'veracious' (accurate account of story events) and 'coherent' (makes sense of text). A punchline may force an interpretation that improves coherence without being factually correct in the story-world; audiences need not adopt it as fact but must recognize it as a possible coherent perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism is media-independent (verbal, visual, mixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinterpretation mechanisms occur across media (words, cartoons, actions) and are not tied to syntactic/semantic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comic strip revealing wider view, Marx Brothers scenes where punchline is visual though set-up verbal. When analyzing or creating jokes, map the same reinterpretation logic onto different media rather than relying solely on linguistic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity can be lexical, syntactic, pragmatic, or non-linguistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources of multiple readings include lexical ambiguity (e.g. 'tank'), illocutionary/pragmatic ambiguity (riddle format), narrative misinterpretation by characters, and interpretation of non-linguistic events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or engineering a joke, identify which level(s) of ambiguity provide alternative readings; the paper's examples demonstrate all these types (1)-(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish audience reinterpretation vs character misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinterpretation may be triggered by the audience revising their own interpretation or by recognizing that a character in the story has misinterpreted events (and the audience represents that character's viewpoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (3)-(6) show character-based misinterpretation. Analysis should state whose viewpoint changes (audience, narrative viewpoint, or character viewpoint) because this affects what the audience needs to accept to achieve coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint-based representational constructs required
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical machinery: viewpoint (mental space), accessibility relation (nesting), counterpart relation, event-sequence, individual, interpretation, contributes relation, and a viewof function linking individuals to their viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper recommends using these abstract constructs (close to Fauconnier's mental spaces/ViewGen) to represent how interpretations and reinterpretations are structured. Use diagrams showing BEFORE and AFTER configurations (PSU, PPL, I_SU, I_PL, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default principle: counterparts in subordinate viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Default assumption: contents of one viewpoint are deemed to have direct counterparts in a subordinate (accessible) viewpoint unless evidence to the contrary exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling stories, assume story-world objects and interpretations are available as counterparts to characters' viewpoints by default; revise explicitly when punchline contradicts that default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up and punchline contribute to overall interpretation via links
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the set-up interpretation and the punchline interpretation link (via M and contributes relations) to an overall interpretation of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent the mapping from presentation event-sequences (PSU, PPL) to interpretations (I_SU, I_PL) and their contribution to I_ALL. In analyses or computational models, make these linking relations explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-prioritize verbal/referential taxonomy over mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Although verbal vs referential (or visual vs non-visual) is a useful distinction, it should not be given disproportionate importance because the same reinterpretation mechanism can cut across these categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomies that split jokes by medium risk missing cross-medium generalizations about the reinterpretation mechanism. Classify primarily by the interpretive dynamics rather than surface medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous material is often embedded (practical guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous material crucial to the set-up will often be embedded (e.g. in a character's utterance or a cited piece of text) rather than asserted directly by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing forced-reinterpretation jokes, embed the ambiguity in utterances or objects within the narrative to make the later reinterpretation plausible; note: example (1) refutes an earlier conjecture that this is always the case, so treat this as a common but not absolute pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological recommendation: use data abstraction, avoid heavy formalism-lock-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocated approach: postulate just the constructs needed from knowledge-representation theories (mental spaces, belief logic) without embedding the analysis tightly into one particular formal theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For both theoretical clarity and portability, model forced reinterpretation using minimal abstract primitives (viewpoints, accessibility, counterparts) and delegate representational specifics to the chosen formalism later. This prevents the humor analysis from being obscured by formalism-specific technicalities.
